# Page 3^page=3
In tro ductio n Anyone can use this manual to learn about Unit 1, from starting it up to operating it. It is filled with images to help you locate components and operate them. This guide covers the Classic reactor type only. It assumes you have sufficient rod fuel and that the unit doesn't have any major malfunctions. The startup checklist also assumes the reactor is in a shutdown state with no emergency systems active. This rookie-friendly guide teaches how to operate panels manually (without the autocontrols) in Unit 1 MCR . There will be sections that cover the use of autocontrol, but the majority of this guide will focus on manual control. Please note that this manual does not guarantee a successful startup. If you still run into trouble in the game, such as being stuck on a step in the guide or questioning something, you can reach out to the communications server in the #ask-an-instructor channel. Once you get the hang of Unit 1, you might want to try Unit 2 as well! If you identify any inaccuracies, discrepancies within the guide, outdated content, or missing images, or if you have suggestions for improvement, please contact one of the authors listed on the first page. First, we will cover what a boiling water reactor is. Afterwards, a checklist for starting up the reactor and running up the turbine at 20% APRM, followed by a detailed breakdown of each component, including manual control. Make sure to check the quick reference for the startup checklists, as they contain useful and vital information.

# Page 4^page=4
Boiling Water Reactor (BWR) In this reactor, the water is allowed to boil directly in the reactor, and as heat rises, the steam rises to the top into the steam separators to remove any moisture from the steam which improves the efficiency of the turbine. The steam is sent to the turbine which is used to spin it to 3600 RPM and, in turn, the turbine generator , which produces electricity. To control power boron control rods enter the core from bottom to top. Due to the steam separators being in the way, control rods can’t enter from top to bottom. Since this raises safety concerns (gravity trying to pull them out), HCU accumulators and redundant systems are used to force the control rods back into the core. Reactor recirculation pumps are used as another method to raise reactor power . In the core there are steam bubbles in the water (less water per bubble) and since water acts as a moderator (slows neutrons down increasing the chances of a fission occurring) the recirculation pumps replace those bubbles with water therefore there is more moderation and more reactivity and power rises. Since water is boiling in the core, if it was left unchecked, the reactor water level would be too low and cause a meltdown. Feedwater pumps are used to replace the boiled water and maintain the reactor water level. Once the steam is used by the turbine it gets condensed back into water and is pumped by the feedwater pumps restarting the cycle. In RBWR there are multiple stages to this cycle, discussed later. You need to consider the chemical makeup of your reactor. A byproduct of nuclear fission, Iodine-135 will rise to the current APRM reading. Iodine-135 doesn’t affect the reactor but it later decays into Xenon-135 which is a neutron absorber, acting as a poison. If too much Xenon builds up the reactor may be difficult to start up. You can “burn” Xenon at high reactor thermal powers. Xenon decay is only a concern after an abrupt shutdown.

# Page 10^page=10
Quick Referen ce: Reacto r Startup C hecklist 4. Reactor period is used to measure how fast your reactor power is changing. The closer the absolute value is to 0s the faster the power is changing. A positive period means the power is increasing, and a negative period means the power is decreasing. Make sure to keep the period above 25s while withdrawing by either reducing the rod control speed or ceasing withdrawal entirely. If the absolute value goes below 20s , it will trigger a reactor SCRAM. 5. When your IRM is at or above 70% , increase the IRM level by one. If it is below 25% , decrease the IRM level until it is within the normal range. Additionally , you may set the IRM level to 6 and ignore it if you wish. Once the IRM level reaches 6, you may disregard it.

# Page 11^page=11
Quick Referen ce: Turbin e Run up C hecklist 3. To enable the Turbine Main Valve, RCIC must be off, and there must be proper condenser vacuum with the reactor water level being below 3.5m . 6. Main Vlv. Setpoint (Turbine CV) is used to control the turbine RPM and the steam pressure. As the turbine RPM approaches 3600, decrease the Turbine CV by a minor amount so that the RPM acceleration slows down as it continues to approach 3600. If the RPM is above 3600, decrease the Turbine CV until the RPM starts decreasing. 7. To synchronize the turbine, the RPM must be between 3595 and 3605, and the phase angle (displayed on the synchroscope ) must be pointing upwards (at the green light). The phase angle will rotate counterclockwise if the RPM is less than 3600, and it will rotate clockwise if the RPM is above 3600. Adjust your RPM using the Main Vlv. Setpoint (Turbine CV) until the phase angle is near the green light, then enable the Gen. Breaker switch so that the turbine is synced and is magnetically locked at 3600 RPM. You may enable Auto Accel. and configure it to “Fast” speed for 3600 RPM if you have trouble syncing. 8. Your Electrical Distribution Panel should look like this:

# Page 12^page=12
Meetin g the D eman d In order to earn points for Unit 1, you have to meet the demand given by the grid, which changes every 12-20 minutes, by keeping the absolute value of the Network Difference below 50 MW. Autocontrols and certain conditions cause you to earn fewer points. Meeting Plant Demand provides 0.2 p/s for both units. The numbers in parentheses represent the total value of both units combined.

# Page 13^page=13
Ho w to Meet the D eman d 1) Check the current demand from the Network Manager Monitor . 2) Network Demand is the current demand given by the grid, and you must be within 50 MW of it to earn points. ○ If the Network Difference is higher than 50 MW, you must lower the power . ○ If it is lower than -50 MW, you must raise the power . 3) Change the power by using the rods or the recirculation pumps. ○ It is advised to first bring the APRM to 30% or above by using the rods before increasing the recirculation pump speed above 30% . ○ If the recirculation pump speed is below 30% , insert the rods to decrease the power instead of decreasing the recirculation pump speed. ○ Once the average rod position reaches 100% , use the recirculation pumps to increase power . ○ Automatic Reactor Control: ■ Rod Mode: Use below 30% APRM (controls the rods). ■ Recirc Mode: Use above 30% APRM (controls the recirculation pumps). 4) When changing the power , make sure to operate components that are not under automatic control, such as the turbine, MCC, and condenser . ○ Automatic control cannot handle every scenario. Regularly monitor automated systems to verify they are operating within safe parameters. ○ The optimal steam pressure is 7100 kPa. Adjust the steam pressure using the Main Vlv. Setpoint. 5) Earning Points: ○ When your Network Difference is within 50 MW, your unit is meeting the demand and earning points for all active players. 6) Plant Demand: ○ To meet the Plant Demand, both units must meet their respective Network Demands. ○ When the number in parentheses on the Network Difference is within 50 MW, you are meeting the total plant demand. ■ This number represents the Network Difference of both units added up. Do not use the Turbine Bypass after synchronization unless necessary. Bypass usage wastes the steam, resulting in decreased power efficiency and triggering a point penalty .

# Page 14^page=14
Ho w to Earn Mo re Po in ts You can check how many points per second you are earning from the Points Information Panel monitor , which will show you points per second/minute/hour , total points generated, and automatic control information. The more autocontrols you have active, the fewer points you will earn. The timer next to the autocontrol status shows the cooldown required in seconds before the point penalty stops. Enabling autocontrol automatically resets this timer to 300 seconds. Note that a misconfigured deaerator incurs the same penalty rate, while successfully meeting Plant Demand awards 0.2 points per second for both units. Events, inspections, and plant evacuation drills give instant points. Please note that events and plant evacuation drills occur at the start of the next demand cycle. Inspections can only be done by people with the rank of Inspector or higher, and plant evacuation drills can only be done by people with the rank of Senior Inspector or higher. What C auses Po in t Pen alties ● Turbine Bypass above 5% or steam relief enabled. ● Automatic controls. ● Deaerator misconfigured. ● Steam pressure not between 6500 kPa and 8000 kPa.

# Page 15^page=15
Emergen cy Systems There are various emergency systems located in Unit 1, such as the Steam Relief Valve, Emergency Diesel Generator , RCIC, and LPCI . The purpose of these pieces of equipment is to cool the core by injecting cold water and to handle emergencies, such as low water levels or loss of offsite power . This section will go over what they do and when you should enable them. Steam Relief Valve [SRV] System Overview The Steam Relief Valve (SRV) provides rapid depressurization of the reactor vessel by venting the steam away, resulting in a decrease in steam pressure. ● Primary Function: Will rapidly decrease the steam pressure. ● Location: Turbine Control Panel. ● Note: SRV results in decreased steam flow to the condenser and a loss of total water inventory . You have to enable Hotwell Makeup to maintain the total water volume. When to Use SRV is utilized when the steam pressure is too high. ● Depressurization: When the steam pressure is above 8 MPa. ● Enabling LPCI: Helps decrease the steam pressure in order for LPCI to function.

# Page 16^page=16
Emergen cy D iesel Gen erato r [ED G] System Overview The Emergency Diesel Generator (EDG) is the primary backup power source for Bus S during a Loss of Offsite Power (LOOP) event. ● Target Speed: The power supply becomes available only once the EDG reaches 1800 RPM. Startup Procedure Follow these steps to start up the EDG and energize Bus S: 1. Energize Bus DC: Ensure it is energized via AC-DC 2 BUS DC or Breaker 52DC1 . 2. Enabling the Startup Spark: Close Breaker 52DCG , then enable Startup Spark to run up the EDG. 3. Run Up: Wait for the EDG speed to reach 1800 RPM. 4. Close Breaker 52G1. ○ Bus S will now receive power from the EDG. Closing Breaker 52G1 will open Breaker 52BA3 and vice versa. These breakers cannot be closed simultaneously .

# Page 17^page=17
Reacto r C o re Iso latio n C o o lin g [RC IC ] System Overview RCIC utilizes an independent, steam-driven turbine to provide emergency cooling to the core. ● Location: Emergency Core Cooling System Panel. ● Power Source: None (Relies on steam). ● Requirement: Sufficient steam pressure. Operating Principles The relationship between steam and feedwater is directly proportional to the Inlet Valve position: ● Higher Steam Pressure: Faster turbine rotation and increased feedwater flow. ● Inlet Valve Opening: Increasing the valve position provides more feedwater flow but causes a decrease in steam pressure. ● Note: The RCIC turbine requires time to spool up and down. When to Use RCIC is specifically designed for no power or low water situations. ● Loss of Power: When the offsite connection is severed. ● Low Water Level: When the water level drops below -4m. The Turbine Control Panel is rendered ineffective immediately upon RCIC activation; neither of the valves will have an effect as long as RCIC is active. Enabling RCIC will cause a turbine trip to occur, and it will disable the feedwater pumps in favor of RCIC.

# Page 18^page=18
Lo w Pressure C o o lan t In jectio n [LPC I] System Overview LPCI is utilized to inject large amounts of coolant into the reactor during emergencies. ● Location: Emergency Core Cooling System Panel. ● Power Source: Bus S (Energized via EDG or Bus A). ● Requirement: Steam pressure under 3 MPa. When to Use LPCI should be used in the case of low water situations. ● Alongside RCIC: For a bonus coolant injection. ● Low Water Level: When the water level drops below -4m. NOTE: In Unit 1, RCIC and LPCI get the water from an infinite source, so they can run indefinitely . However , in Unit 2, they get the water from the Condensate Storage Tank (CST) .

# Page 19^page=19
Reacto r C o n tro l Since the reactor is how you generate steam, it is one of the most important components within Unit 1. This section will explain everything on the Reactor Control and Recirculation Panel and will demonstrate how to operate them manually. Reacto r C o n tro l Pan el This panel is used to control the rods and to monitor the reactor power , such as APRM, SRM, and IRM.

# Page 20^page=20
A - Vertical Ro d D isp lay This display will show you the temperature of different rod levels. On average level, if a cell is red, it's too warm and should be inserted, and if it is blue, it's too cold and should be withdrawn. You can adjust which level to see from the Rod Level (K). Balancing the rod temperatures is optional and does not provide any bonus points. B - A verage Ro d Po sitio n This display will show the average position to which the control rods are withdrawn. C - Ro d Po sitio n D isp lay This display will show the rod positions as well as rod powers. D - SRM (So urce Ran ge Mo n ito r) SRM is used during startup to monitor the neutron count when APRM and IRM are unable to show accurate readings. E - IRM (In termediate Po wer Ran ge Mo n ito r) IRM is used after the SRM phase and before the APRM phase. The IRM must be kept between 20%-70% during startup. If it is too high, increase the IRM level; conversely , if it is too low, decrease the IRM level. You can adjust the IRM level from the IRM Level Control (O). F - Reacto r Perio d The reactor period is used to measure how fast the power is changing. A positive period means the power is increasing, and a negative period means the power is decreasing. INF means the power is stable. The lower the absolute value, the more rapidly your power will change. If the value of the reactor period drops below 20s, an automatic reactor SCRAM will be triggered. Withdrawing control rods or increasing the recirculation pump speed will result in a shorter (faster) positive period. Conversely , inserting rods or slowing the pumps will lengthen the positive period toward infinity and will eventually result in a negative period. G - A PRM (A verage Po wer Ran ge Mo n ito r) After your IRM goes above 50% on level 6, you will get an APRM reading. APRM is used to monitor your reactor power after startup. If APRM goes above 125%, it will SCRAM the reactor. Rods and recirculation pumps are used to adjust the APRM.

# Page 21^page=21
H - Gen erato r Lo ad This display will show the power output of the generator in megawatts. This does not include your house load, meaning your unit’s power consumption is not taken into consideration. To meet the demand, this should be greater than the Network Demand by a minor amount (40-60 MW). I - A uto B alan cer Sp eed Auto Balancer will monitor the rod temperatures from the Vertical Rod Display (A) and insert/withdraw rods to balance their temperatures while keeping the power stable. The speed determines how fast it will balance the rods, and OFF means it is disabled. Since balancing the rods gives no point bonus, it is advised to keep this off to avoid unnecessary point penalties. J - Ro d C o n tro l Mo de & Ro d C o n tro l Sp eed Rod Control Mode is separated into “Group” and “All”. Group mode will only allow the control of the rods that are selected on the Rod Matrix (L), and All mode will control all of the rods. Rod Control Speed will change how fast you withdraw/insert the rods. Faster speed will result in swifter power changes. K - Ro d Level Rod Level will adjust which level of the reactor the Vertical Rod Display (A) will show. It is advised to keep this on A (average) for optimal rod temperature monitoring. L - Ro d Matrix Rod Matrix allows you to select multiple rod cells that can be either withdrawn or inserted if the Rod Control Mode (J) is set to “Group”. M - Man ual SC RA M Manual SCRAM will rapidly insert all of the rods to decrease the power and shut down the reactor instantly. Manual SCRAM is used during emergencies such as low water level or Loss of Offsite Power. While you can manually SCRAM the reactor, autocontrol can also SCRAM the reactor automatically if it is in a dangerous state. You cannot bypass automatic SCRAMs. Scramming a fully withdrawn rod takes ~26 seconds.

# Page 22^page=22
N - Ro d C o n tro l Rod Control allows you to withdraw or insert the rods. This is the primary way of controlling the reactor power . If Rod Control Mode (J) is on “Group”, it will only control the highlighted rods on the Rod Matrix (L). Withdrawing will increase the power , and inserting will decrease it. O - IRM Level C o n tro l IRM Level Control is used during the IRM phase to keep the IRM between 20%-70%. Increasing the level will decrease the IRM, and vice versa. It can be increased to a maximum level of 6. Recirculatio n C o n tro l Pan el Recirculation pumps increase the power by decreasing the amount of steam bubbles inside the reactor vessel. To enable a recirculation pump, enable its starter, inlet, and outlet switches. Bus A must be energized for the recirculation pumps to function. Increasing the recirculation pump speed will increase the power , and vice versa. In RBMK, it's the opposite: increasing the recirculation pump speed will decrease the power , and vice versa. Do not exceed 30% recirculation speed below 20% APRM, since it will cause pump cavitation.

# Page 23^page=23
B alan ce Of Plan t (B OP) Op eratio n s Balance of Plant covers all but the reactor and its emergency systems. This section explains multiple components and how to manually control them for increased points. D eaerato r In real life, the deaerator removes dissolved gases from the feedwater to avoid corrosion. In RBWR, the deaerator is only operated to give bonus points while meeting the demand and has no negative impact on the reactor if it is misconfigured. How to Manually Operate the Deaerator: There are 2 values you have to monitor: deaerator temperature and deaerator pressure . Inlet Valve ● Used to control the deaerator temperature . ● Directly affects the deaerator temperature. Also directly affects the deaerator pressure to a minor extent. Outlet Valve ● Used to control the deaerator pressure . ● Inversely affects the deaerator pressure. If the deaerator level increases, the deaerator pressure will increase. Conversely , if the deaerator level decreases, the deaerator pressure will decrease. You can almost always keep the Gas Outlet at 70% and adjust the Steam Inflow accordingly to get the deaerator temperature to 108°C . If the deaerator pressure is too low or too high, adjust the Gas Outlet accordingly. Do not lower the Gas Outlet below 50% ; otherwise, it will cause ineffective deaeration and trigger the misconfiguration point penalty. You should only configure the deaerator while meeting the demand, since it doesn’t contribute to anything if you aren’t meeting it.

# Page 24^page=24
C o n den ser The condenser condenses the steam coming from the bypass and turbine back into water and stores it in the hotwell so that it can be reused. How to Manually Operate the Condenser: There are SJAEs, CARs, and condenser recirculation pumps . These will decrease the condenser pressure depending on their speed. Your goal is to keep the condenser pressure at ~55 mbar in order to prepare and maintain the turbine. To do that, you have to use an SJAE and both condenser recirculation pumps. Condenser pressure that is too low (causes Off-Gas to open) or too high will cause a turbine trip. CARs are used during startup when there is no steam flow through the condenser to decrease the condenser pressure, and they will automatically turn off below 850 mbar. To get a condenser vacuum before turbine run-up at 20% APRM , you should do the following: 1. Enable SJAE 1 at 100% speed. 2. Enable both cond. rec. pumps at 20% speed (adjust as required). After that, as the condenser steam flow increases, you’re going to have to increase the cond. rec. pump speed to decrease the condenser pressure. Conversely , as the condenser steam flow decreases, you’re going to have to decrease the cond. rec. pump speed since the condenser pressure will decrease. If your condenser pressure gets extremely low, it will cause the Condenser To Off-Gas to open, and it will increase the condenser pressure significantly. This makes it almost impossible to get a condenser vacuum. To fix it, turn off all SJAEs and cond. rec. pumps and wait until the condenser pressure rises significantly so that the annunciator gets turned off. Afterwards, you may enable them again in order to get a condenser vacuum.

# Page 25^page=25
Turbin e C o n tro l The Turbine Control Panel consists of the Turbine Bypass (Bypass Valve) and the Main Vlv. Setpoint [Turbine Control Valve (TCV/CV)] . The purpose of this panel is to control steam pressure and operate the turbine to meet demand and energize Bus B. Turbin e C o n tro l Pan el C o mp o n en ts: The Turbine Control Panel is located to the right of the Recirculation Control Panel . Turbine Bypass (Bypass Valve) ● Used to control steam pressure while the turbine is offline or during runup. ● Must be closed after synchronization to avoid a point penalty. ● Opening decreases steam pressure, and vice versa. Main Vlv. Setpoint [Turbine Control Valve (TCV / CV)] ● Used to control turbine speed (unsynced) and generator load (synced), as well as steam pressure. ● Opening will always lower the steam pressure and, if it is synchronized, will also increase the generator load. Conversely , closing will always raise the steam pressure and, if it is synchronized, will also decrease the generator load. ● Can only be operated when the Turbine Main Valve switch is enabled Turbine Main Valve ● Allows the Turbine CV to be operated. ● Must remain enabled during turbine operations; otherwise, a turbine trip will occur. ● Must meet requirements to be enabled (page 26). Synchroscope ● Displays the phase angle required to synchronize the turbine with the grid. ● Rotates counterclockwise if the turbine speed is lower than 3600 RPM. ● Rotates clockwise if the turbine speed is greater than 3600 RPM. ● When it is pointing upwards (at the green light), you may synchronize the turbine if the turbine speed is within range. Generator Breaker (Gen. Breaker) ● Connects the generator to the electrical grid, magnetically locking the turbine speed at 3600 RPM and synchronizing it. ● Can be enabled once the turbine speed is within 3595-3605 RPM and the phase angle is pointing upwards (at the green light).

# Page 26^page=26
Turbin e C o n tro l Pan el Op eratio n s Use these Turbine Bypass setpoints before turbine runup to maintain a steam pressure of 7100 kPa at specific power levels. Reactor Power (APRM) Turbine Bypass Setpoint 10% APRM 40% Bypass 20% APRM 70% Bypass 30% APRM 100% Bypass Your Tasks: ● At all times, you should be aiming to keep the steam pressure around 7100 kPa. Do not exceed 7300 kPa and don’t go under 5000 kPa. ● Before the turbine is active, you should maintain steam pressure using the Turbine Bypass . ● While running up, use the Turbine Bypass to adjust the steam pressure and the Turbine CV to control the turbine speed. ● After synchronization, remember to fully close the Turbine Bypass to avoid a point penalty and wasting the steam. ● Once the turbine has been synchronized, adjust the steam pressure using only the Turbine CV . If you are having trouble starting up the turbine or synchronizing it to the grid, you may enable Turbine Acceleration (Turb. Accel): ● Turb. Accel. will only function if the Turbine Main Valve is enabled and all of the switches on the panel are on neutral. ● It will automatically adjust the turbine speed to the selected setpoint whilst also adjusting the steam pressure, with its aggressiveness depending on the chosen speed. Faster speed means reaching the setpoint faster. ● It will also adjust the turbine speed if it is within the synchronization range in order to adjust the phase angle correctly. ● It will not function if the turbine is synchronized. If something is wrong, they will light up and emit a sound cue to warn the operators. ● Red annunciators indicate critical failures that require immediate attention and must be resolved swiftly. ● Yellow annunciators signal abnormal conditions or system warnings that should be monitored but do not pose an immediate threat. ● White & Blue annunciators indicate a pump or an autocontrol is active. These are purely for information and do not require intervention. For more information on how to respond to specific annunciators within Unit 1, refer to the “Unit 1 Annunciator Response Procedures” document made by Dopar , located in the RBWR thread within the #official-guides forum.

Ho w to Ran k Up : To rank up, you must earn points by meeting the demand, completing events, participating in inspections/plant evacuations, and refueling. You may gather more information on when you are going to rank up by calling RBWR HR (0100) . Once you have enough points to rank up, you will get a notification that you need to go to the Human Resources room. The HR room is located on the first floor of the building, near the main entrance. Talk with the NPC inside the room to rank up.

Ensure the startup transformer breaker is closed. ○ If offsite power isn’t available, start up the EDG or interlock if possible. 2. Recovering from a Turbine Trip 1. Ensure the startup transformer breaker is closed. ○ If offsite power isn’t available, start up the EDG and either interlock or SCRAM the reactor. 2. Ensure the bypass is open and use SRV as necessary to maintain steam pressure at 7100 kPa. 3. Maintain water level with feedwater pumps or RCIC and LPCI ○ Refer to the Emergency Systems section for more information. Once the reactor has been stabilized and if you have sufficient steam pressure, you may restart the turbine. What C auses an A uto matic SC RA M to Occur: If any of these conditions happen during reactor operation, an automated SCRAM will be triggered, which cannot be bypassed: ● Reactor water level falling below -4m. ● Steam pressure exceeding 10 MPa. ● The absolute reactor period going below 20s. ● APRM increasing above 125%. ● Offsite Event happening while the APRM is above 50%.

Recirculation Panel ● Recirculation Pump ○ The flow of the recirculation pump is calculated by multiplying its speed by 5. If the flow doesn’t match, that pump is malfunctioning. C o mmo n Mistakes: Here are some common mistakes new players make; try to avoid them: ● Forgetting to set a switch to neutral. ● Exceeding the turbine speed above 3600 RPM. ● Not turning off the Bypass Valve after turbine synchronization. ● Not closing Bus A and Bus B transformers after turbine synchronization. ● Letting the steam pressure exceed 8000 kPa. ● Forgetting to enable Bus B required pumps. ● Enabling any CST pump for an extended period whilst on the startup transformer .
